title: Warped galaxies place a tight limit on a dark fifth force
topic: Gravity & Fundamental Physics / Cosmology & Early Universe
freshness: Preliminary preprint submitted October 17, 2026; not yet peer reviewed; found within the preferred 15-day window.
excerpt: Nearly 4,000 edge-on galaxies show no shared warping pattern expected from a force acting on dark matter but not stars. The resulting limit is less than 0.17% of gravity for forces reaching at least 8 megaparsecs, after accounting for tested systematic uncertainties.
whyItMatters: The equivalence principle has been tested with ordinary matter to extraordinary precision, but a force confined to the dark sector could evade those experiments. Galaxy shapes offer a way to test whether dark matter and stars respond differently across cosmic distances.
whatToExploreNext: How could future galaxy surveys separate fifth-force warps from bends produced by gas pressure, tides, dust, and feedback?

sources.label: Desmond and Ferreira, Galactic warps constrain equivalence-principle violation in the dark sector

body:
## Looking for unequal falls in the dark

If dark matter feels an extra force that stars do not, the difference could bend an entire galaxy. A new analysis searched for that distortion in thousands of edge-on disk galaxies and found no matching pattern. The absence gives a tight upper limit on a proposed interaction between dark matter and dark energy.

The idea starts with the equivalence principle: gravity should accelerate objects in the same way, regardless of what they are made of. Laboratory and Solar System experiments test that rule extremely well for ordinary matter. They cannot directly exclude a fifth force that couples only to dark matter.

Such a force would pull a galaxy's dark-matter halo toward surrounding cosmic structure while leaving its stars behind. Because the stellar disk remains gravitationally bound to the halo, it would settle slightly off centre. The halo's restoring pull is weaker in the outskirts, so stars farther from the centre would be displaced more. Seen edge-on, the disk would form a shallow U whose direction follows the predicted dark-matter force.

Harry Desmond and Pedro Ferreira measured this U-shaped component in Sloan Digital Sky Survey images. Their starting catalogue held 4,345 thin, edge-on disks within 250 megaparsecs. After image-quality and catalogue cuts, 3,968 galaxies remained. They then reconstructed the surrounding matter field and predicted the size and direction of each galaxy's warp for a given fifth-force strength and range.

Real disks bend for many ordinary reasons, including tides, gas pressure, stellar feedback, dust, and imperfect viewing geometry. The model treated those competing effects as noise and included corrections for a disk's own gravity, atmospheric blurring, and the projection of a three-dimensional galaxy onto an image. Mock-data tests recovered injected signals without biasing the upper limits downward.

## A missing pattern becomes a measurement

The observed warps did not align with the predicted fifth-force field. At a force range of 8 megaparsecs, the main model limits the extra attraction to less than 0.077% of Newtonian gravity at 95% credibility. The authors also built a more cautious envelope across changes to the halo profile, disk dimensions, gas content, foreground-star masking, and sample cuts. That conservative limit is 0.17% of gravity.

The local matter reconstruction directly supports tests from 0.4 to 8 megaparsecs. For longer ranges, the authors use analytic reasoning and additional calculations out to 20 megaparsecs to argue that the constraint should strengthen rather than weaken. They therefore carry the 0.17% limit into the effectively infinite-range case. Under that extrapolation, it is about three times tighter than the cited cosmological bound and roughly two orders of magnitude tighter than earlier astrophysical limits.

This does not prove that dark matter obeys the equivalence principle in every possible theory. Screening mechanisms or interactions with a different mathematical form could evade the test. The result also depends on models of galaxy halos, baryonic warps, and the reconstructed environment. The authors stress that their conservative envelope is not a standard credible interval from one model.

The work is a preliminary preprint and has not yet passed peer review. Its useful lesson is methodological: a null correlation across many messy galaxies can probe a force too selective for ordinary gravity experiments.

**Measured:** 3,968 galaxy images show no supported correlation between U-shaped warps and the predicted dark-sector force field.

**Inferred:** within the tested model, any long-range fifth force acting only on dark matter must be weaker than about 0.17% of gravity after the authors' systematic allowance.
